entry: American television [[Sitcom|sitcom]] (1977–1984). Developed by Don Nicholl, Michael Ross and Bernie West, it was based on the British sitcom *Man About the House* and ran on ABC for eight seasons, from March 15, 1977, to September 18, 1984. The series follows three single roommates who share a Santa Monica, California, apartment: Jack Tripper, Janet Wood and Chrissy Snow. Its farce of misunderstandings, social lives and financial struggles was a top-10 hit from 1977 to 1983. Spin-offs included *The Ropers* and *Three's a Crowd*, and the show remained popular in syndication and through [[DVD]] releases.

Sexual activity involving three people at the same time. In [[Human sexuality|human sexuality]], a threesome is a sexual interaction in which at least one participant engages in physical sexual behavior with both of the others. At times the term has also described a long-term domestic relationship, such as [[Polyamory|polyamory]] or a *ménage à trois*. A threesome is a form of [[Group sex|group sex]] that typically occurs in private, such as among three friends or in casual sex. It is a common element of [[Sexual fantasy|sexual fantasy]] and is widely depicted in [[Pornography|pornography]].

Sixth studio album by American singer [[Michael Jackson]], released in November 1982 by Epic Records. It was produced by [[Quincy Jones]], who had also produced Jackson's previous album, *Off the Wall* (1979). Its sound blends post-disco, synth-pop, funk and rock, and [[Paul McCartney]] is the first credited featured artist on a Jackson album. It was Jackson's first number-one album on the Billboard Top LPs & Tape chart, where it spent a record 37 non-consecutive weeks at number one. The singles "Billie Jean" and "Beat It" topped the Billboard Hot 100. The album won a record eight [[Grammy Awards]], and by early 1984 it had become the best-selling album of all time. Its music videos, including the one for the title track that premiered on [[MTV]], are credited with transforming music videos into a serious art form. It is estimated to have sold 70 million copies worldwide.

Genre of fiction in literature, film and television, defined by suspense. Thrillers are characterized by the moods they evoke: excitement, surprise, anticipation and anxiety. Plots build toward a climax, and devices such as red herrings, plot twists, unreliable narrators and cliffhangers are used extensively. The genre overlaps with subgenres including crime, horror and [[Detective fiction|detective fiction]]. A distinct style emerged in the 19th and early 20th centuries, with novels such as *The Count of Monte Cristo* (1848) and *The Thirty-Nine Steps* (1915). [[Alfred Hitchcock]] described suspense as an audience expecting something bad to happen while powerless to intervene, and his films were critical to the development of the thriller film in the mid-20th century. In lectures at [[Cornell University]], [[Vladimir Nabokov]] noted that the villain of an Anglo-Saxon thriller is generally punished.

Family of [[Passerine|passerine]] birds with a worldwide distribution. Thrushes are plump, soft-plumaged, small to medium-sized birds that often feed on the ground, taking insects, worms, land snails and fruit. Most species are gray or brown. Many are resident in warm climates, while others migrate long distances to higher latitudes in summer. Thrushes build cup-shaped nests, usually on branches, and lay two to five speckled eggs; both parents help raise the young. Turdidae species also disperse seeds, aiding the recovery of ecosystems. The family was once much larger, until the chats and [[European robin|European robins]] were reclassified as [[Old World flycatcher|Old World flycatchers]]. The family was introduced as Turdinia in 1815 by French [[Polymath|polymath]] Constantine Samuel Rafinesque.

Type of reverse [[Fault (geology)|fault]] with a dip of 45 degrees or less. A thrust fault is a break in the [[Earth's crust]] across which older rocks are pushed above younger rocks. If the fault plane lies at a shallow angle, often less than 15 degrees from horizontal, and the overlying block is displaced far, the fault is called an overthrust. Erosion can expose the underlying block as a small window, or fenster, or leave isolated remnants called klippen. A blind thrust fault ends before reaching the surface and is hard to detect before rupture; the destructive 1994 earthquake in Northridge, Los Angeles, California, was caused by one. Thrusts often follow a ramp-flat geometry, and where a thrust climbs a ramp, a fault-bend fold forms.

5th-century BC Athenian historian and general. He wrote the *History of the Peloponnesian War*, which chronicles the war between [[Sparta]] and [[Athens]] up to 411 BC. Regarded as the father of "scientific history" for claiming strict impartiality and evidence-gathering, he explained events without reference to the gods. He is also called the father of political realism, which holds that relations between states rest on fear and self-interest. The Melian dialogue is regarded as a seminal text of [[International relations|international relations]] theory, and his version of the funeral oration by [[Pericles]] is widely studied. He survived the [[Plague (disease)|plague]] that struck Athens and killed Pericles. Blamed for the fall of Amphipolis to the Spartan general Brasidas in 424–423 BC, he was exiled for twenty years.

Chemical element with symbol Tm and [[Atomic number|atomic number]] 69. It is the thirteenth element of the [[Lanthanide|lanthanide]] series and the second-least abundant lanthanide in the Earth's crust, after radioactive [[Promethium|promethium]]. It is a soft, easily worked [[Metal|metal]] with a silvery-gray luster that tarnishes slowly in air. Despite its high price and rarity, thulium is used as a dopant in solid-state lasers, and artificial radioactive isotopes serve as radiation sources in some portable [[X-ray|X-ray]] devices. In 1879 Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve separated thulia from the rare-earth mineral erbia, and the metal itself was first obtained in 1936. Like other lanthanides, it most commonly has oxidation state +3. It has no significant biological role.

Sound caused by [[Lightning|lightning]]. Depending on the distance and nature of the lightning, thunder can range from a long, low rumble to a sudden, loud crack. The lightning channel reaches about 30,000 K, and the resulting rapid expansion of the air produces a sonic shock wave, often called a thunderclap. Near the source, thunder usually measures 165 to 180 dB. Ancient Greek philosophers attributed it to natural causes: [[Aristotle]] to wind striking clouds, and [[Democritus]] to air moving within them. The scientific study of thunder is called brontology.

Storm characterized by [[Lightning|lightning]] and [[Thunder|thunder]], also called an electrical storm. Thunderstorms occur in [[Cumulonimbus cloud|cumulonimbus clouds]], which can rise over 20 kilometers (12 mi), when warm, moist air rises rapidly, often along a front. They are usually accompanied by strong winds and often produce heavy rain, sometimes snow, sleet or [[Hail|hail]]. Damage is mainly caused by downburst winds, large hailstones and [[Flash flood|flash flooding]]. There are three types: single-cell, multi-cell and [[Supercell|supercell]] storms, the strongest and most severe. Stronger cells can produce [[Tornado|tornadoes]] and waterspouts, and dry thunderstorms can start [[Wildfire|wildfires]] from cloud-to-ground lightning. Thunderstorms have been observed on Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and, probably, Venus.

Landlocked state in central [[Germany]]. Its capital is Erfurt, and it covers 16,171 square kilometers (6,244 sq mi). The modern state was established in 1920 by the [[Weimar Republic]] and became part of the German Democratic Republic in 1949, but was dissolved in 1952. It was re-established in 1990 following [[German reunification]]. Thuringia was the birthplace of, or favored by, three key intellectuals and arts leaders: [[Johann Sebastian Bach]], [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]] and [[Friedrich Schiller]]. As of 2014, Thuringian athletes had won half of Germany's 136 Winter Olympic gold medals.

Day of the [[Week]] between Wednesday and [[Friday]]. It is the fourth day of the week under the ISO 8601 standard, and the fifth under the Sunday-first convention. The English name derives from Old English *þunresdæg*, named after the Old English god Thunor, whose name and that of [[Thor]] come from the Germanic god of thunder. In most [[Romance languages|Romance languages]], the day is named after [[Jupiter (god)|Jupiter]], as in Italian *giovedì* and Spanish *jueves*. In [[Hinduism|Hindu]] tradition, the day marks the worship of [[Vishnu]] and is linked to Bṛhaspati, guru of the gods.

[[Pharaoh]] of [[Egypt]] (r. 1479–1425 BC). Sometimes called Thutmose the Great, he was one of the greatest warriors of his time. For the first 22 years of his reign he was coregent with his stepmother and aunt, [[Hatshepsut]], who was named pharaoh; he became sole ruler after her death around 1458 BC. He conducted between 17 and 20 military campaigns, all victorious, which brought Egypt's empire to its zenith. The campaigns are detailed in the *Annals of Thutmose III*. He also created the ancient Egyptian [[Navy|navy]], the first navy in the ancient world. Historian Richard Gabriel called him the "[[Napoleon|Napoleon]] of Egypt". Dates follow the Low Chronology, the conventional academic chronology since the 1960s.

Extinct carnivorous [[Marsupial|marsupial]], also known as the Tasmanian tiger or Tasmanian wolf. Formerly native to mainland [[Australia (continent)|Australia]], [[Tasmania]] and [[New Guinea]], it became extinct on the mainland and in New Guinea about 3,600–3,200 years ago, possibly after the [[Dingo|dingo]] arrived. In Tasmania, 19th-century government bounties targeted it as a threat to livestock. The last known individual died at Hobart Zoo on September 7, 1936. Its name derives from the Greek *thýlakos*, meaning "pouch", and it was the only member of its genus to survive into modern times. Its relatives include the [[Tasmanian devil]]. Intensive hunting is blamed for its extinction.

Culinary herb made from the dried aerial parts of some species of *Thymus*, in the mint family [[Lamiaceae]]. Thymes are native to Mediterranean countries in [[North Africa]], the [[Levant]] and southern Europe, and have culinary, medicinal and ornamental uses. Common thyme (*Thymus vulgaris*), native to southeastern Europe, is the most widely cultivated species. [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] used it for embalming, and the Greeks burned it as [[Incense|incense]] in their temples, believing it was a source of [[Courage|courage]]. In the [[Middle Ages]], thyme was placed under pillows to aid sleep. Oil of thyme, the essential oil of common thyme, contains 20–54% thymol, a compound historically used as an [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]] and antiseptic. Thyme is a component of *bouquet garni* and *herbes de Provence*.

Butterfly-shaped endocrine gland in the neck, below the Adam's apple. It weighs 25 grams in adults and is usually larger in women than in men.The thyroid secretes two hormones, triiodothyronine (T3) and thyroxine (T4), which influence metabolic rate and growth, and calcitonin, which plays a role in calcium homeostasis. Its secretion is regulated by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the [[Pituitary gland|anterior pituitary]]. Hyperthyroidism most often results from Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder. [[Hypothyroidism]] most commonly results from [[Iodine|iodine]] deficiency. In iodine-deficient regions it is the leading preventable cause of [[Intellectual disability|intellectual disability]] in children, while in iodine-sufficient regions Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause.

System of mountain ranges in [[Central Asia]], sacred in Tengrism. The range extends about 2,900 kilometers east from [[Tashkent]], Uzbekistan, and straddles [[Kazakhstan]], [[Kyrgyzstan]], Uzbekistan and China's Xinjiang region. It lies north and west of the [[Taklamakan Desert]]. Its highest peak, Jengish Chokusu, rises to 7,439 meters (24,406 ft) on the Kyrgyzstan–China border. Khan Tengri, the second-highest peak, reaches 7,010 meters (23,000 ft) and is the highest point in Kazakhstan. The range forms part of the [[Himalayas|Himalayan]] orogenic belt, produced by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates in the Cenozoic era. The [[Syr Darya]] and Tarim rivers originate here. Its glaciers have lost 27% or 5.4 billion tons of ice since 1961, nearly four times the global average of 7%.

Public square in central [[Beijing]], China. It is named after the Tiananmen gate to its north, which separates it from the [[Forbidden City]]. The square holds the Monument to the People's Heroes, the Great Hall of the People and the National Museum of China. [[Mao Zedong]] proclaimed the People's Republic of China here on October 1, 1949. The square was enlarged fourfold in the 1950s and measures 765 × 282 meters (215,730 m²). Outside China it is best known for the [[1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre|1989 protests and massacre]], which the government strictly censors within China.

Chinese modular [[Space station|space station]] in [[Low Earth orbit|low Earth orbit]] since 2021. Operated by the China Manned Space Agency, it is China's first permanently crewed space station. Its core module, Tianhe, launched in April 2021. Crews of three fly aboard Shenzhou spacecraft. Experiments have included atomic clocks, [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose–Einstein condensates]] and the agricultural cycle of rice. After the U.S. Wolf Amendment barred Chinese participation in the [[International Space Station]], China developed its own station, which has hosted the first astronaut from [[Hong Kong]]. China is also training astronauts from [[Macau]] and [[Pakistan]]. It is the third modular station, after [[Mir]] and the ISS.

Coastal municipality of [[China]] on the Bohai Sea (pop., 2020: 13,866,009). It borders [[Hebei|Hebei Province]] and [[Beijing]] and is the largest coastal city in northern China, part of the Jing-Jin-Ji megalopolis. The name, meaning "ford of the emperor", is most often attributed to the [[Yongle Emperor]] of the [[Ming dynasty|Ming]] dynasty, who crossed the Gu River here. A walled city was built in 1404. As a treaty port from 1860, it served as a seaport and gateway to Beijing, and during the [[Boxer Rebellion]] it was the seat of a provisional government. After 1949 it declined, hit by the [[1976 Tangshan earthquake]], but has recovered since the 1990s. Since 2010 its Yujiapu Financial District has been called [[Manhattan|China's Manhattan]].

City on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee in northern [[Israel]] (pop., 2024: 52,123). Considered one of [[Judaism|Judaism]]'s Four Holy Cities since the 18th century, along with [[Jerusalem]], [[Hebron]] and Safed, it was founded around 20 CE by Herod Antipas and named after the Roman emperor [[Tiberius]]. From the 2nd through the 10th centuries CE it was the largest Jewish city in Galilee, where much of the Mishna and the Jerusalem [[Talmud]] was compiled. During the 1947–1948 civil war in [[Mandatory Palestine]], British troops evacuated the Palestinian Arab population, which was refused reentry after the war, leaving the city almost exclusively Jewish.

[[Roman emperor]] (r. AD 14–37). The second emperor, he succeeded his stepfather [[Augustus]] and was the second ruler of the [[Julio-Claudian dynasty]]. Before his accession he was an able diplomat and one of the most successful Roman generals; his conquests of Pannonia, Dalmatia and Raetia laid the foundations of the empire's northern frontier along the [[Danube]] and [[Rhine]]. He had a difficult, resentful relationship with the Senate and suspected many plots. After the deaths of his nephew Germanicus (AD 19) and his son Drusus (AD 23), he withdrew from Rome in AD 26, leaving administration largely to the praetorian prefect Sejanus, who was executed for treason in AD 31. He was succeeded by his grand-nephew [[Caligula]]. [[Pliny the Elder]] called him "the gloomiest of men".

Autonomous region of [[China]], established in 1965. It replaced the Tibet Area, a former administrative division of the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]], and includes about half of cultural [[Tibet]]. Its borders were generally set in the 18th century. Covering more than 1,200,000 sq km (460,000 sq mi), it is China's second-largest province-level division by area. Its population of 3.6 million averages about 3 inhabitants per sq km. The official Chinese name, Xizang, means "Western Zang", while Zang refers broadly to Tibet and Tibetan culture.

Region of western [[East Asia]] covering much of the [[Tibetan Plateau]]. It is the homeland of the [[Tibetans]], who share the plateau with [[Mongols]], Monpa, Qiang, Sherpa and others. Its average elevation is 4,380 m (14,000 ft), and its highest point, [[Mount Everest]], lies in the Himalayas at 8,848 m (29,000 ft). The Yarlung dynasty expanded in the 7th century, and by the 9th the [[Tibetan Empire]] stretched from the Tarim Basin to Yunnan and Bengal. Central Tibet was autonomous until 1951, when after the Battle of Chamdo it came under the People's Republic of China. Most of the historical area is now the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]] and autonomous prefectures in neighboring provinces. Tibetan Buddhism is the dominant religion. Human rights organizations report restrictions on religious practice, expression and assembly, although the extent of these restrictions is debated.

Power centered on the [[Tibetan Plateau]] from 618 to 842. Formed under the Yarlung dynasty's 33rd king, Songtsen Gampo, in the 7th century, it reached its greatest extent under Tritsuk Detsen, stretching from Chang'an in the east, beyond modern Afghanistan in the west, and south into India and the Bay of Bengal. Under Trisong Detsen, Guru [[Padmasambhava|Padmasambhava]] helped establish Tibetan Buddhism and [[Vajrayana]] in Tibet. A treaty with the [[Tang dynasty]] in 783 defined the borders. The empire began to dissolve after Tritsuk Detsen was murdered in 838 by his brother Langdarma, who was himself assassinated in 842. Langdarma nearly destroyed Tibetan Buddhism through his widespread targeting of Nyingma monasteries.
